speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As the global economic landscape changes, we correspondingly updated our economic strategies and developed new competitive advantages and capabilities to ride on the prevailing opportunities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In our earlier post-Independence years, we started off competing as a low-cost manufacturing location, attracting multinational corporations (MNCs) to set up in Singapore while at the same time also growing our own timber by building up home-bred companies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Complementing our strength as an entrepot, we built up export-led industrial capabilities augmented with a skillful workforce.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the 1980s and 1990s, we further moved up the value ladder, creating value-adding hubs, such as manufacturing, petrochemicals, financial services, shipbuilding, air and sea transportation, among others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We also encouraged local enterprises to go regional and seek growth through internationalisation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By any measure, our economic development has been a great success.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It has progressed the country, created good jobs, incomes and opportunities, brought about a better quality of life and strengthened our financial security.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fast forward to today, the operating context has once again changed and, this time round, with fast disruptive implications.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The rise of anti-globalisation sentiments and the inward-looking policies of the new United States (US) administration are real and present concerns, although we do hope that these changes are not permanent and can improve over time.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But what is of more consequence to us are the permanent and irreversible changes that are taking place even as we speak.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, the global value chains are being restructured and, as a result, we have seen international trade slowed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Countries like China and the US are in-sourcing more than before due to availability of better production technologies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This has direct and indirect impacts on manufacturing, shipping, port and other supporting sectors where we have built up strong capabilities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the overriding reason why it is the time again to reposition our economy is the rapid technological changes that are fast disrupting businesses, products, services, the value chain and the way we earn our living.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What this means is that we have pretty much plucked most of the lower hanging fruits or even the middle hanging fruits.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From here on, our next unit of growth would have to come from plucking the higher hanging fruits which may well taste better.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In CFE lingo, this is what we meant by moving from value-adding to value-creating or, in the case of internationalisation, encouraging our enterprises to move beyond the traditional markets into more challenging international markets to seek further business growth.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Well, it sounds like a new economic strategy is needed and here enters CFE and its recommendations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to do the "single or double jump", so to speak, in terms of overall capabilities so that these higher hanging fruits are within our reach.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is doable and we can build on our existing advantages.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What I like about the CFE report is the "true to ourselves" way that it sums up the global and domestic realities that we face today and in the future, and the no-frills but pragmatic way in which it outlines what needs to be done to get to the new promised land.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even if we could get just some of these efforts to bear fruits, we would have moved or pushed the frontiers forward.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In some of these key thrusts, we may need to start in small steps initially to gain traction.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thereafter, we scale up fast so as to multiply the value and move the needle.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: ITMs clearly demonstrated this grounded and microeconomic-centric approach.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, ITMs need to have the space and the risk tolerance to experiment new ideas and also necessarily empowered to make speedy ground decisions to respond to fast-changing industry scenarios.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope that the whole exercise of CFE has also uplifted businesses' enthusiasm and confidence to embrace the new future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government can and should help, support, facilitate and enable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we also know that too much of it can also be counterproductive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Already, I felt that the Government's hand is everywhere to be seen within the economy, not to mention the extensive assistance schemes and support offered by agencies like the Standards, Productivity and Innovation Board (SPRING), International Enterprise (IE) Singapore and others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ultimately, it is still the businesses that will come up with the next "killer" product or services that can sell to the consumers of the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How does the Government plan to implement these recommendations?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can the Government help companies capture these growth opportunities?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How has the partnership between the Government and TACs progressed?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can TACs play a bigger role, moving forward?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fifthly, we have been building up our startup landscape for some time now.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What more does the Government plan to do to enable the startup scene to be vibrant and continue to grow?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Mr Chairman, Singaporeans today enjoy a standard of living that is comparable to that of most advanced economies in the world.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: This has been made possible by our sustained economic growth through the years.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: We have also weathered several economic crises in our short history.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Significant recent examples of these are the Global Financial Crisis at the end of the last decade, the bursting of the Dotcom Bubble in the early 2000s and the Asian Financial Crisis in the late 1990s.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Each time, we have come out of these crises more resilient, and we learn lessons from them and diversify our economy.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: While the global economy seems to be recovering from the most recent financial crisis, growth is projected to be subdued and lower than in the previous decade.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Furthermore, the events that took place last year in the United Kingdom (UK) and in the US point to a world that is turning increasingly inwards.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: This is a worrying trend, which seems to have found some traction in some other countries, including a number in continental Europe.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: While a move away from globalisation will likely hurt all economies, small and open ones like Singapore's will be hit particularly badly, as our fortunes are inextricably tied to the rest of the world's.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: For example, our gross domestic product (GDP) growth averaged 5% from 2001-2010, despite the bursting of the Dotcom Bubble at the start of that period and the Global Financial Crisis at the end of the decade.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Mr Chairman, the effects of this have, however, been felt by Singaporeans and many residents I have spoken with in my constituency they have told me that they are personally feeling the pinch of the slower growing economy.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: With this in mind, I would like to ask the Minister for Trade and Industry to elaborate on the outlook for Singapore's economic growth in the short to medium term and how it will continue to create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Faced with a modest outlook for the coming year, I am concerned about the risks to growth from the rise of anti-globalisation sentiment, Brexit, uncertainties about the Trump administration's economic policies and the possibility of a sharper than expected slowdown in China.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, we do see that Asia remains to be a bright spot, driven by infrastructure development and e-commerce.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What challenges and opportunities does the Minister see for Singapore and Singaporeans, amidst these developments?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What measures are being rolled out by our Government to help the nation navigate the external uncertainties, including trade policies?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How can our firms and individuals position themselves to thrive under these conditions?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Should we be hopeful, Minister, that the pickup in the fourth quarter will endure and that Singapore has turned the corner?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: On the ground, people are worried about their job security.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many businesses are struggling with the effects of globalisation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Labour market constraints and high cost of doing business remain key challenges.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The business community complains about the rising compliance costs and that Singapore has grown less flexible and competitive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They also hear about the ambitious developments in neighbouring countries and worry that Singapore risks being marginalised.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Some economists have gone as far as labelling Singapore as the "new sick man of Asia".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Notwithstanding the comprehensive set of recommendations by CFE, there is no silver bullet and many of the proposed initiatives take time to take effect, requiring significant efforts from all stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister about his assessment of the outlook of Singapore's economy for the next two to three years?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: While CFE is focused on the long-term economic transformation, is there more that the Government can do to manage key business costs, such as rentals?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We have seen rental costs decline considerably for industrial land, and Jurong Town Corporation (JTC) seemed to have made some downward adjustments.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But there could be room for the Government to do more to influence the retail market rental.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Should the retail slump worsen, as a short-term counter-cyclical measure, could the Government consider reducing property tax for retail real estate, on condition that the property tax savings get passed entirely to the operating businesses?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Today, I would like to focus on the cost of regulations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: An SME owner Mr Ong told me this story.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One day, as he drove past some roadworks, he saw two men digging a pit, two men supervising, one with a blue helmet, another with a white helmet.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: A guy sitting on the excavator waiting to start work, with a signalman and a rigger man on standby for the excavator to start digging, plus two signalmen to direct traffic.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Nine men in total to dig a hole.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I explained that this work process seemed to comply with the Building and Construction Authority's (BCA's) requirements.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am sure some of us have heard construction company owners speaking of their frustrations keeping up with regulations, mandatory training for their workforce, shortage of labour quota and so on.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am not so familiar with the construction industry.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: So, I did a check on some of the compliance requirements.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Please bear with me as I run through some of them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Under the Contractors' Registration System (CRS), there are seven major groups of registration heads, namely, Construction Workheads (CW), Construction-Related Workheads (CR), Mechanical and Electrical (ME), Maintenance (MW), Trade (TR), Supply (SY) and Regulatory (RW).

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Contractors and subcontractors only need to register in CRS if they wish to participate in public works and tenders.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, this may not help the smaller companies.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: CRS is further divided into seven major categories − Construction (CW), Maintenance (MW), Supply (SY) and so on.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In total, there are 63 workheads, and each of them has their own special requirements.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Smaller construction companies may find it difficult to find the right heads, let alone fulfil the strict requirements.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As a result, many construction companies have resorted to collaborating with one another to make use of their professional certificates to tender for projects.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This may sound like a joint venture, but it is not.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Borrowing of certificates drives up costs and compromises the intended objectives of CRS.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There are many regulations from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), JTC, the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA), BCA, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM), the National Environment Agency that the business owner must try to understand and comply with.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For the large companies, they have the infrastructure and the capital.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, for smaller companies, the multitude of regulations take capital and energy away from innovation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am not suggesting that we do away with regulations but they are there for a purpose.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In doing so, we could lower the compliance costs for some SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Yet, a significant number of SMEs continue to cite the need for Government assistance relating to business rental.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Quite apart from the fact that no assistance is too much assistance as far as prospective recipients are concerned, it seems that businesses facing challenging times may find even falling business rental a substantial burden.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: And for SMEs in some sectors more than others, business rental makes up a significant part of their operating costs.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: There are good reasons for this: to help SMEs relieve some of the pressure they feel and better take on the challenges of restructuring and drive innovation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In survey after survey, year after year, escalating business costs have been cited as a perennial bugbear for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In its Budget recommendations for 2016 and 2017, SBF highlighted that there was an urgent need to assist SMEs with business costs in the immediate term so as to help them overcome near-term economic headwinds, and high rental costs have consistently ranked among the top cost concerns for businesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The study should also include how the cost of doing business in Singapore compares globally, identify areas where the Government can provide greater support to our local businesses, and provide concrete recommendations in this regard.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Only by having a deep understanding of the factors that cause rental costs to escalate can we incorporate the lessons into our long-term strategy and avoid crushing rental surges in future.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng, do you want to take both cuts together?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our workers ‒ our brothers and sisters − are concerned about the Marine and Offshore Engineering sector.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Oil prices are not what they used to be.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is a sense of uncertainty in the industry.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Any job losses will affect workers, breadwinners, families.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Retrenchments would also hurt the industry as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When a worker is let go, skills are lost, institutional memory is lost.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And what more is the Government planning to do?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For some sectors like e-commerce and e-payments, platform interoperability matters.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But more generally in other sectors, too, a shared operating system benefits all the participants − less back-office paperwork for vendors, ease of use for customers and a scalability of the user base and opportunities.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, I would like to ask: how is the Ministry working with regional partners and collaborators to build shared industry standards − almost a shared operating system − to deepen regional cooperation to benefit the different regional partners and our local businesses as well?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: GDP growth for developed economies is stagnating and fewer investments are taking place amidst the uncertainties around the world.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In the past decade, Singapore's economy has been dependent on global trade.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And this is likely to remain as we continue to be constrained by a lack of natural resources and small domestic consumption.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Political themes around the world are leading to a lot of uncertainty and could become game changers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But one thing that is certain is that free trade has invariably changed when viewed with the same lenses.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If we look at the two powerhouses globally − the US and China ‒ their plans and developments have huge implications on the global economy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Any fiscal stimulus and deregulation from these countries will result in a domino effect through the value chain.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They may be at the early stages before formal negotiation with the European Union (EU), but their potential departure has tipped the iceberg after a ripple effect amongst the countries in the EU.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In the US, Trump's growth agenda seems to focus on three areas: short-term fiscal boost through lowering taxes for companies, domestic deregulation in the energy and healthcare sector, putting America first in foreign trade policy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This discussion of a new tax regime for companies have actually brought about mixed reactions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Moving ahead, it is clear that China cannot sustain its growth using previous policies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They have made announcements on a policy shift towards stability and industrial production growth.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With these changing policies from our large trading partners, how will this impact Singapore?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If so, how are we reviewing our existing free trade agreements (FTAs) and developing new ones?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Also, what industry sectors are more likely to be affected?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: We also built on our position as a gateway to the region and to become an important hub for businesses.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: However, the global trade landscape is fast changing.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: At the same time, the Committee also called for Singapore to strive to remain open and connected to the world.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: I, for one, agree that it is even more important today to stay open and be connected.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: But it will be challenging for us to do so in this current climate.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: How can we improve on our Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)-centric FTAs and what is next in terms of Singapore's trade agreements?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Will Singapore enhance existing bilateral FTAs and build new ones?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have very good diplomatic relations and trade with many of the Asian countries and our neighbouring ASEAN countries, which is a good start.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can local businesses tap on these opportunities and how will the Government support them?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am hoping for more proactive measures of creating jobs and directing overseas projects, particularly those in construction and infrastructure planning, to the local companies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I had also mentioned in the Budget speech about building up our next generation in regional languages and cultures, so that they can connect easily with the regional counterparts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides the SkillsFuture Leadership programme, how much more can we do for the future generation of business leaders?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their comments and suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The US economy is projected to grow at a faster pace, primarily supported by domestic demand.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Growth in the Eurozone is likely to remain modest, while China's economic growth is expected to ease on the back of its continued restructuring.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The global outlook also remains clouded with uncertainties and downside risks.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Upcoming elections in key Eurozone economies may pose uncertainties regarding the direction of the monetary union.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: If anti-globalisation sentiments and protectionism take root, global trade will be adversely affected.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Political risks and uncertainty in the new US administration's policies have also led to greater economic uncertainties and financial market volatility.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: These factors could, in turn, weigh on business and consumer confidence, dampening investment and consumption.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: At the same time, technological changes continue to gather pace, disrupting entire industries even as they create new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Many of these changes are still playing out and it is difficult to know with certainty how things will develop.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: So, against this backdrop, the Singapore economy as a whole is on a stable and steady growth trajectory.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Mr Charles Chong observed that the growth rates have come down in recent years.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: As CFE has highlighted, we have to adapt to a lower but more sustainable rate of 2% to 3% growth as our economy matures and undergoes structural adjustments.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Mr Charles Chong asked about the outlook in the short and medium term.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We have narrowed our productivity gap with other advanced economies, although there is scope for improvement, especially for domestically-oriented sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Over this period, the productivity of outward-oriented sectors, such as manufacturing, wholesale trade and finance and insurance, have increased by 2.7% per annum, while that of the domestically-oriented sectors, such as construction, retail and food and beverage (F&B), grew by 0.7% per annum.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: As our restructuring efforts gather momentum, we can expect to see steady progress in achieving our productivity targets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Wage growth has been comparable to or higher than many advanced economies, in part due to the tightness in our labour market.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Between 2010 and 2016, real median gross monthly income of full-time employed residents grew by 3.1% per annum.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: At the same time, the annual average resident unemployment rate has remained low, at 3% or lower since 2011, while the resident labour force participation rate has remained high.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: So, despite the difficult conditions that we are facing, our labour market is holding up.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Third, despite an uncertain environment, we remain globally competitive.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The World Economic Forum's Global Competitiveness Report 2016-2017 ranked Singapore as the second most competitive economy in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We continue to attract a steady pipeline of investments, thus creating new job opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: These investments are expected to create an average of 20,000 jobs annually when the projects are fully implemented.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har observed that despite the 2% growth in 2016, business sentiments remain weak.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: One reason for this is the uneven performance across different segments of our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Growth in the sector was led by the semiconductor segment, which grew by 31% in 2016 and, to a lesser extent, the machinery and systems segment, which grew by around 5%.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: On the other hand, the marine and offshore engineering segment continued to contract.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Similarly, the printing and the miscellaneous industries segments of the general manufacturing cluster saw a drop in their output last year.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: It is thus not surprising that while firms in the semiconductor and machinery and systems segments are positive about their business prospects, firms in the marine and offshore, printing and miscellaneous industries segments would feel pessimistic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Similarly, even though the services sectors on the whole saw subdued growth in 2016, there continues to be bright spots, such as in information technology (IT) services, education, health and social services.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: On the other hand, the retail trade segment will continue to face structural challenges as it adapts to e-commerce and weak consumer demand.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Even within the same sector, the performance of firms was also uneven.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: For example, within the logistics sector, firms with major contracts from the marine and offshore engineering segment were harder hit.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Conversely, firms that had a diverse portfolio of clients from different industries, especially those that provided more integrated and specialised value-added services, did better than the industry average.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: This uneven performance across our economy and the uncertain economic outlook explain the weak business sentiments and the sense of insecurity among our workers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Recognising that there are different opportunities and challenges for each sector, the ITMs are the right approach to address the specific needs of each industry.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The Government will continue working with our businesses and unions to overcome challenges that we are facing.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: First, we introduced several initiatives at Budget 2016 to support our companies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: They are still relevant and effective in dealing with the current situation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: With the improved credit availability under this scheme, our SMEs can better address their cash flow concerns and their growth financing needs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Another initiative is the Automation Support Package (ASP), which complements SPRING's existing Capability Development Grant in helping companies achieve productivity improvements.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: In 2016, these two schemes collectively supported 226 automation projects.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: An example of a company that has benefited from this scheme is Commonwealth Culinary Creations Pte Ltd (CCC).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Through the use of automation, CCC improved the quality, consistency and range of their confections.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Their output per shift doubled, even though they used less manpower than before.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: This allowed CCC to scale up and take on larger business opportunities as well as supported its long-term goal to expand regionally and to the Middle East.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Second, the Government closely monitors our economy and stands ready to take decisive action if needed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Both aim to stabilise the M&OE sector as it copes with prolonged weaknesses in oil prices.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng asked if the support measures have been successful.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: As of February 2017, applications amounting to more than $90 million of loans have been approved.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Based on feedback from participating financial institutions, we expect the pipeline demand to be strong, with more than 100 companies already indicating interest in the scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The access to financing will help companies finance their operations, bridge short-term cash flow gaps and take on new projects.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Stabilising the industry will help to preserve Singapore's core capabilities in the sector and save jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: With the stabilisation of oil prices, we are beginning to see some upstream and mid-stream activities taking place in the oil and gas sector.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: There is, of course, a certain amount of lag in the sector, so some of the suppliers and stockists may not feel the impact as yet.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: But anyway, the Government continues to monitor the sector closely and we track indicators, such as order books and output levels in the sector, and we continue to evaluate the feedback from industry players.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Third, we will continue to keep a close eye on business costs to ensure that they do not rise excessively.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: For the services sector, the unit business cost index increased at a more moderate 0.1% year-on-year for the first three quarters of 2016, compared to an average 0.5% increase per annum of the four years before that.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Mr Henry Kwek, Ms Cheng Li Hui, Mr Chen Show Mao and Mr Dennis Tan spoke about rental costs, which are a component of unit business cost.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: First, we have to understand the contribution of rental costs for the different sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We do acknowledge that SMEs in the retail sector and in the F&B sector, rental cost, as a share of their total business costs, is around 30% and is, therefore, significant.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: But for the other sectors, rental cost is not so significant.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: For example, in the manufacturing sector, rental cost is a small share of total business cost at between 0.7% and 4.8%.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Similarly, in most services sectors, rental cost constitutes around 5% of business cost.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Second, in the last three years, the rentals have been declining in all the various sectors ‒ industrial space, commercial space, retail and office.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: So, the problem has not been so severe in the last three years.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Third, the Government believes in letting market forces set the rent and we allow the private sector to provide the responses in supplying the demand.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Where we intervene is where we recognise some possible market failures.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: For example, in startups where it is not so commercially viable to provide the space, the Government will step in and, indeed, we have.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: JTC set up LaunchPad@one-north in 2015 and plans to build a network of LaunchPads around Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The next one will be completed in the Jurong Innovation District this year.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: JTC has also been developing industrial facilities with shared services for SMEs in order to reduce their capital expenditure and operational costs in such specialised facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Mr Henry Kwek suggested reducing property tax for retail real estate.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: This will not help most of our retailers because the landlords would benefit directly and it is very difficult for the Government to instruct landlords to pass on the tax savings to tenants.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: This is a sustainable way to manage business costs, rather than through direct intervention through rental rebates.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Mr Chairman, let me now turn to the medium- and long-term challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We are confident that Singapore is well-positioned to seize opportunities of the future.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: CFE has identified two key thrusts − first, remaining open and connected and, second, building deep capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked how our strategy of remaining open and connected will serve us, given the rise of anti-globalisation sentiments globally.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Small and open economies like Singapore are especially vulnerable to global developments but, at the same time, our external linkages can also make us more resilient.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Our trade connections across the world have enabled our companies to access new markets and cutting-edge technology and have created good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: So, going overseas allows us to tap into the higher growth potential of Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: When companies internationalise, about 60% of jobs created are for professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMET) jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: So, internationalisation helps us to create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how we can support our companies to tap on overseas opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Our trade agreements also lower other barriers to trade.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Under the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC)-Singapore FTA, there is mutual recognition of halal standards.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: This means that a product that is halal-certified by the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (MUIS) does not have to go through additional halal certification processes when it enters the GCC countries.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: So, this provides added certainty for companies which export products to the GCC countries.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan and Mr Lee Yi Shyan also asked what is next for our trade agreements, and Dr Tan Wu Meng asked how we are working with our regional partners to deepen cooperation on standards.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Under the ASEAN Economic Community, ASEAN member states are looking at the harmonisation and mutual recognition of standards across a wide range of sectors, including automotives, cosmetics and medical devices, and aligning them to international standards wherever possible.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We are also working with our ASEAN member states to improve trade facilitation through the ASEAN-wide Self-Certification regime and the ASEAN Single Window (ASW).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: These initiatives will also reduce the administrative burden and cost to our traders.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We will also press on with our efforts for greater regional connectivity through the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We will also ensure that our agreements meet our changing business needs, especially in the digital economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Common trade rules governing e-commerce will promote greater digital connectivity in the region by reducing barriers to e-commerce and improving security of electronic transactions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: All these will be introduced and incorporated in our new trade agreements.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The second way we can support our companies is by deepening our linkages at the provincial, state and city levels.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We can do so through bilateral platforms and government-to-government (G-to-G) projects.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: In China, Singapore companies have made inroads through our seven provincial business councils.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Our third G-to-G project, the Chongqing Connectivity Initiative (CCI) will also enable us to engage the provinces in western China.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: As provinces and cities within a country will differ in strengths and challenges, we also adapt accordingly.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: For example, the Vietnam-Singapore Industrial Park (VSIP) projects are spread across six provinces in Vietnam and cater to the priorities of each province, taking into account the locals' skillsets as well as investors' demand.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: So, Singapore food companies, for example, have set up in VSIP 1 in Binh Duong province in southern Vietnam to cater to the growing middle class and the expanding demand for premium food products.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Meanwhile, companies in electronics manufacturing and logistics services have set up in VSIP 3 in Bac Ninh province in northern Vietnam to support the increased presence of consumer electronics MNCs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: We should also deepen our engagements at the city level.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: For instance, in Indonesia, Bandung and Makassar are keen to incorporate digital solutions in their city development.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: With IE Singapore's assistance, a Singapore e-government solutions company, Ecquaria, set up a software development centre in Bandung and is in discussions with the Bandung City Administration on the provision of e-government services.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: IE Singapore also signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Makassar to facilitate Singapore companies in providing Smart City solutions and technology.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: There are also opportunities to be seized in developed markets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Singapore has hosted delegations from US states like Texas, Alabama and Washington, all of whom have been eager to find new markets for their exports and welcome new investments.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: At the same time, there is interest from Singapore companies to invest in the US.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: So, working closely with our economic agencies, we will identify mutually beneficial partnerships at the state level.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The third way we will support our companies is by strengthening our internationalisation efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The digital economy presents opportunities for SMEs to access new markets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: They have now developed their own e-commerce platform, Kinofy, to serve as a marketplace for health and beauty products targeted at the Chinese market, and this platform will soon be supporting products from other companies as well.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: In addition, Singapore companies can partner larger companies to venture abroad.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: InvitroCue, a home-grown biotechnology firm that was spun-off from the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), provides cell-based models for global pharmaceutical companies to test drug and medical devices.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Singapore companies enjoy greater economies of scale by going abroad together.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: TACs play a unique role in such collaborations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Last year, the Singapore Manufacturing Federation (SMF) and IE Singapore partnered our companies to help them collectively obtain lower product listing fees and better shelf displays, as well as organise promotional activities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: SMF also helped to oversee the consolidation of our companies' exports, shipping them to the supermarkets in shared containers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Through this collaboration, our companies were able to bring their products overseas at a lower cost, compared to if they had done so themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The final way which we will support our companies is through the Global Innovation Alliance (GIA), as announced by the Minister for Finance.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: The future economy will be characterised by a global network of innovation and talent.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Cities which are plugged into this network will have a strong advantage.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: By linking our enterprises and students with overseas partners in major innovation hubs and key demand markets, our companies and people will benefit from the opportunities as well as the overseas exposure.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Similarly, Singapore can also tap on the best global talent and ideas to stay at the forefront of innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: GIA's focus in each city will be tailored according to its strengths.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: In cities like San Francisco and Beijing, where there are thriving, world-class innovation ecosystems, we want our students and companies to be immersed in the environment and to be able to interact with them.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: In cities like Jakarta, innovation ecosystems are just rapidly taking shape and our companies should, therefore, be participating in these developments.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Minister Iswaran and Minister of State Dr Koh Poh Koon will explain how our SMEs and startups can benefit from this initiative.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Mr Chairman, over the years, Singapore has adopted a consistent and deliberate strategy to remain open and connected.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: This has opened up new opportunities for our businesses and people, even during challenging times.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: Amidst the uncertain operating environment, we are convinced that staying the course remains the right thing to do.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (Mr Lim Hng Kiang)
text: An open and connected Singapore will be better placed to tap on the opportunities of the future economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: ITMs integrate planning and implementation, bringing together industry partners, TACs, unions and public agencies.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: What results have been achieved and what lessons have we learnt?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: How can we fast-track the implementation of the other ITMs and ensure that they are implemented successfully?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: The Minister for Finance shared that ITMs are "live" plans that will be adjusted along the way.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: We are in uncharted waters, with no blueprint or map to lead the way forward.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: And, together, we will feel our way through.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: TACs have been identified as playing a pivotal role in helping their respective sectors transform and scale up.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: During my Budget speech, I highlighted the pivotal role, the great example that MAS has played in creating the enabling environment for the finance sector.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The reality is that firms go into the discussion with different perspectives.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Big firms wonder what is in this for me?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will there be discussion into who and what the potential disruptors to my business will be and what I should do?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will there be investments into new areas of growth and how can I benefit from that?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Small firms wonder will there be honest sharing of best practices?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will I get to know more suppliers, more customers to help grow my business and will the Government help with grants to make my return on investment from using new technologies and new processes more appealing?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With such dynamics in place, how do we bring firms together to share the strengths that work for them and which could be trade secrets and also for firms to be honest about their weaknesses?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I suggest that the economic lead agencies conduct in-depth one-to-one discussions to thoroughly understand the corporates and what they need.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To avoid being constrained by local models and local environment when putting together the ITMs, I suggest that disruptors, entrepreneurs from adjacent industries and overseas markets be brought into the ITM discussions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Resource panels can be set up to ensure that there are systematic exploration and follow-up on their inputs.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, setting the parameters for ITMs is going to be a crucial part of positioning the firms for success.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: From the CFE report, it was recommended that Singapore continue to build a globally competitive manufacturing sector.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Can the Minister provide more details behind the recommendation?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Additive manufacturing sector and robotics automation were cited in the Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE)2020 as cutting-edge technology across different industry verticals.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Additive manufacturing had a long gestation period since the 1980s.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: It has improved and advanced tremendously in the past five years when digitalisation became more widespread and materials improved.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Extensive collaboration and consolidation have been taking place in the industry and this trend would only continue.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The challenge is that global manufacturers like General Electric (GE), Airbus, Bosch, Siemens and so on of the different vertical industries are directly acquiring and investing in leading companies of 3D equipment manufacturers, software platforms and materials for printing.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: With their substantive investments and a strong focus on R&D and vertically integrated manufacturing capabilities, they will be ahead of the industry players when it comes to commercialisation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Will the collaborations we pursue result in a flow-through from research to social and economic impact, which is a key thrust of RIE2020?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Apart from our focus on ITMs, I hope the Ministry in future will take an active review to look ahead at emerging trends and gaps of the different industries so as to facilitate earlier skills training of our workforce and timely introduction of new courses or curriculum within our education system.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Charles Chong, do you wish to take both cuts together?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: The first cut relates to industry transformation and how we can help our businesses lower costs through a practice known as resource pooling.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: The Government has said that industry transformation will require strong partnerships at various levels.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Each ITM is led by a single agency with overall responsibility for coordinating among the relevant agencies.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: This makes very good sense and is less confusing for our companies, who can look to the lead agency for their industry.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: I understand also that the Government wants to work closely with our unions and TACs to promote industry transformation.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: This is also something to be encouraged as these stakeholders can provide valuable feedback, insights and connections to help us with this.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: But apart from these sorts of public-private partnerships, another type of partnership is also needed to take place more often and on a larger scale, namely, partnerships within the private sector.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: For example, businesses, especially SMEs, can consider employing a practice known as resource pooling.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: This refers to the sharing of the purchase cost of big-ticket items amongst companies which need to use it, thus lowering the cost per SME.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: This will help us adopt new technologies, which can sometimes be expensive to adopt without sufficient scale.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Resource pooling amongst businesses has proven effective in raising productivity and lowering business costs.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: However, it remains less common in Singapore, compared to countries like Japan.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: I would, therefore, like to ask the Minister whether ITMs will be able to promote resource-pooling among businesses.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: In my second cut, I would like to address the broader topic of innovation and how we can strengthen our innovation ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: This is very important, because we are entering a new phase of growth that will be increasingly driven by technology and innovation.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: ITMs are a step in the right direction, but transforming industries is not easy, with many stakeholders involved.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: This is why we must get our innovation and productivity strategies right.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: We have done well in the past and, over the years, we have built up a dynamic research ecosystem with excellent research-intensive universities, mission-oriented research institutes under A*STAR, as well as a growing base of innovative local companies.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: The challenge is to do even better, given our slowing workforce growth.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Competition is also intensifying as other countries, including some in this region, are taking steps to increase their attractiveness as innovation hubs.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: More broadly, we must ensure that we have a robust research RIE system in place to complement our efforts under the ITMs.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: In particular, in line with the trend of open innovation, it is important to forge connections and partnerships across public and private sector players in our ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: I would, therefore, like to ask the Minister how we can strengthen our innovation ecosystem so that we can better prepare our companies to keep pace with technological developments.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Could the Minister provide a little more elucidation on what A*STAR's transformation will entail and how A*STAR will be better organised to support the changing needs of industry?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In a competitive environment, we learn from one another.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The more successful one is, the more one is liable to be copied.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The same is true for companies, the same is true for countries.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The easiest competencies for competitors to imitate tend to be those that are tangible, such as infrastructures.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Changi Airport may be visible, such as the Singapore Girl and transactable.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, intangible resources, such as intellectual capital, are harder to imitate.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: For intellectual capital to be effective as our competitive edge and advantage, it must be directed, managed, developed, applied and protected holistically and strategically.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Put simplistically, the durability of our competitive advantage is a function of the speed at which we can be imitated.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In the world that we now live in, it is not just about staying ahead.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened that at the highest level of our leadership, innovation and the prudent management of intellectual property and capital are seen as critical to our survival.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that the agencies designing and implementing the schemes to support innovation will also see that it is a matter of survival for our country.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened that, at the policy level, we could be seeing moves away from expenditure as a key performance indicator (KPI).

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It was a conversation between two ladies, when one contemptuously told the other that a certain Mrs X had yet undergone another facelift.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: When she was asked how she knew, the first-mentioned lady said: "Why, it is as clear as the nose on her forehead!" The point I would like to make, Mr Chairman, is that the devil is in the details and the mindset.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If we make only cosmetic changes or, if we do not execute structural changes rightly, we may end up with a nose on our forehead.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is equally important is to thoroughly review the economic impact of such public sector R&D spending so that we know what is working and what is not.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For instance, which fields of R&D have the highest long-term multiplier effect?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, has this IP helped to create total business spending in the wider economy and, if so, how much.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Running and publishing regular analyses of this nature for Parliament and the public to review would help to ensure that our R&D spending is optimised for economic and other benefits.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such analyses do not preclude some R&D spending going to knowledge creation for intrinsically altruistic and academic purposes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But knowing exactly what the economic impact is makes for greater transparency and better decision-making.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, after the Fukushima nuclear disaster in 2011, DARPA organised a Robotics Challenge that spanned four years, aiming to spur research and technological advancement in the field of disaster robotics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The prize for the fastest robot to navigate an obstacle course based on conditions in Fukushima was $2 million and was won by the South Korean team.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such large-scale competitions do not only stimulate innovation and the progress of the industry, but also encourage the right qualities of perseverance, creativity and teamwork among those in the R&D field.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The resulting intellectual property could be harnessed to benefit the Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I suggest that we make more use of secondments of staff from private companies to the public sector to serve short stints to help with economic planning or promotion initiatives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the UK, the central civil service has just introduced a new framework for managing secondments into and out of civil service jobs, aimed at building meaningful links between the civil service and business leaders.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Britain is also seeking private sector secondees to help prepare for the upcoming Brexit negotiations, which will be technically very complex.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Japan similarly has private sector secondees working in its ministries to quite a significant extent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Singapore, there could be good demand for secondments in both directions, as business executives and civil servants may see the benefits of a stint on the other side.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, there are some potential pitfalls of secondment − ensuring that the stints are not too long or too short, enabling secondees to adapt to a new work culture and so on − but these can be addressed through good human resource (HR) frameworks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given the challenges of a 21st century economy and the predominance of lifelong civil servants in the upper echelons of public organisations and political officeholders, secondments from the private sector could better enable us to form and execute our economic policies.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore, as an open economy that participates in international trade, is highly susceptible to external shocks and changes in business cycles.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: CFE highlighted the importance of innovation, digitalisation and productivity for us to meet the challenges ahead, while the CFE report is mainly targeted at the private sector and there are ITMs to help companies and workers in various industries adapt to the future changes.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Could the Ministry share how the Government and public sector are also adapting?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore's sound regulatory environment has always been an important part of our attractive business environment.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: Our processes and regulations have provided a safe and predictable environment for our people and enterprises.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: However, as the CFE report mentioned, this is an era of rapid technological change.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: The emergence of new business models has upended traditional industries, such as Uber and Grab in the taxi industry, and Airbnb in the hotel industry.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: The Government will need to be nimbler, given the rapid pace of innovation and shorter technology cycles.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: Specifically, our regulations will need to keep up with the speed of industry disruption.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: These should adopt a balanced approach, placing safeguards on the risks in new industries, but also enhancing the ease of doing business.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: What changes will the Government make to ensure that we have an innovation-friendly and agile regulatory environment which supports the growth of promising sectors?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: As part of our pro-business environment, it is also important to have clear and simple regulations to provide a conducive environment for businesses to start and grow.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: Overly complex regulatory processes leave business with less time and money for their actual business activities and this impedes corporate growth and innovation.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: Therefore, besides pushing regulatory innovations in the new sectors, how will the Government ensure that our business regulations are streamlined and simplified to render Singapore most business-friendly against global competition?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan
text: Will the Ministry consider a "Cut Red Tape task force" to greatly reduce layers of regulations added over time by various agencies?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: I also talked about ways to implement regulatory sandboxes, modifying tender systems to give emerging companies with strong ideas a better shot at success.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: And in terms of regulations, leaning towards consumer preferences which are more embracing of the new economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Therefore, I am delighted to hear that CFE recommends using forward-looking regulations and Government-led demand to support innovation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Can MTI provide specifics on how the Government plans to implement these recommendations?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Can MTI also share which are the industries that we expect to see these implemented in?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: More than half of the world live or work in urban areas and this number is increasing significantly every year, especially in Asia.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: This rapid growth, coupled with the rising expectations of the growing middle class, creates significant strains in cities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Singapore is consistently ranked as one of the world's most liveable cities, with strengths in water management, green constructions, smart energy management, greenery management and inclusive urban planning.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: We are also recognised as a global thought leader in this field, with initiatives, such as the Centre for Liveable Cities (CLC) and the Lee Kuan Yew (LKY) School's Water Institute, as well as an increasing number of global conventions and international events, such as World Cities Summit or the Singapore International Water Week.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Indeed, CFE identified urban solutions as one of the growth sectors that would benefit from the rising middle class and urbanisation in Asia.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: As Singapore invents the future, it is important that we bring our companies along this journey.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Can MTI share some of the successful, emerging Singapore-based companies that are successfully doing so in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Moving forward, can MTI share the specific ways in which the Government can do more to help our companies capture these growth opportunities?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, a carbon tax alone will not spur energy conservation and reduce emissions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Industries could prepare for this rise in the next few years, factor in the rise in costs and end up not reducing energy consumption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The only one who would profit then would be the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of the most common tools used in conjunction with carbon taxation or cap-and-trade regimes around the world is the setting of hard targets for renewable energy production, coupled with carbon offset incentives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should cement Singapore's commitment to energy conservation by setting a target for renewable energy production.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These offsets can be partly funded by revenue from the carbon tax revenue in the initial years.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: The SolarNova programme is a step in the right direction, although mainly in public areas of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: As it stands, when electricity from solar energy is exported back to the grid, solar facilities owners will sell the electricity back at a lower rate than the normal electricity price due to the deduction of a grid charge.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: In many other countries, the reverse is true and solar facilities owners can sell the solar electricity at a higher rate than the normal electricity price.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: This is to encourage the adoption of clean energy.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: To encourage more installations of solar and other clean energy facilities, could we consider that grid charges be levied on a one-time basis commensurate with the cost of processing and connecting the facility to the grid, rather than on an ongoing basis?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: I would also like to ask the Ministry to elaborate further on our plans to encourage the use of clean energy in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Next, Chairman, we are introducing a carbon tax on large direct emitters of greenhouse gases from 2019.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: On this note, I would like to suggest implementing a system of tiered charging for electricity based on consumption.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: We can consider setting the tier at a high level, hence we do not penalise the bulk of the households in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Perhaps, we can set a benchmark for only the top 5% to 10% users of electricity for a start.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: The additional revenue can be used to subsidise the lower-income households so as to minimise the impact of the carbon tax on them.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Chairman, I want to thank all the Members who have spoken on the MTI debate so far.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: At the debate on the Budget Statement, I emphasised that we need to gear up our economy and our enterprises so that they can seize the significant opportunities presented by the growth of Asia and the rise of the middle class here.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, I want to now elaborate on the work that MTI and our agencies are doing towards that objective.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The backdrop, as many Members have observed, is a confluence of political, economic and technological trends that is quite unparalleled in recent times.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As many Members have emphasised, anti-globalisation and protectionist sentiments appear to be gaining momentum in the US and Europe.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Global trade and production patterns are changing and the value chains are being reconfigured.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Technological advances are disrupting business models and changing the nature of jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It is increasingly harder to anticipate which sector, enterprise model or job type will be the next to see a major transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For example, the impact today of Uber, the sharing economy and fintech was not fully appreciated as recently as five years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We expect more industries to be "Uberised", but we cannot be sure which ones, when and to what extent.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Given such uncertainty, the most durable strategy is to focus on the fundamentals that will keep Singapore relevant to the world and its needs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is why CFE has emphasised two basic points, Openness and Capability.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Strengthening these fundamentals is the surest way to prepare Singapore for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Minister Lim has already explained how Singapore and how we are growing and showing that Singapore remains connected to the world and open to trade, investments and talent.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: ITMs are a key mechanism to build enterprise capabilities and transform sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Ms Sun Xueling suggested deeper engagements with corporates, Mr Leon Perera enquired how we could involve the private sector more.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I want to use the food manufacturing ITM which was launched in November last year, as an example to address these questions and suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Chairman, may I have your permission to show some slides?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The ITMs integrate the Government policies and initiatives and promote collaboration among industry stakeholders to achieve transformation and growth through productivity, skills development, innovation and internationalisation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
