text: SPRING is the lead agency for food manufacturing and they work with Government agencies and industry stakeholders to develop the ITM.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The goal is to develop Singapore into Asia's leading food and nutrition hub.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There are quantitative targets to galvanise the efforts to realise this goal.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These are, as Members would have acknowledged, quite ambitious targets, especially when we compare with other sectors and historical paths.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The SMEs have been actively involved in the development of the ITM, which also aims to address their needs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For example, many SMEs found the cost of R&D and technology adoption prohibitive because they lack scale.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Therefore, one component of the ITM is to build a network of shared infrastructure to increase productivity and create co-innovation opportunities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: One such shared resource is the high-pressure processing (HPP) tolling facility.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Food in its final packaging is subjected to high levels of pressure to extend shelf life.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The smallest of such machines cost about $800,000, which is not cost-effective for an SME to purchase for its exclusive use.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Food manufacturers will be able to use the machine on a pay-per-use basis.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The ITM also aims to help companies collaborate on innovation with initial focus on MNC-SME projects.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Montreux Patisserie, a local bakery, has partnered Unilever Food Solutions, for example, to develop new flavours and products.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: SPRING has started a Food Innovation Cluster (FIC) Workgroup so that our companies can spawn more of such partnerships with global food innovators and corporate accelerators.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As Mr Charles Chong has emphasised, such resource pooling, whether it is in terms of equipment or R&D effort, can help raise productivity and lower business costs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: However, resource sharing is still a relatively nascent idea for local food manufacturers, and it is important that our business owners be open to such novel business arrangements if we are to succeed in industry transformation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: ITMs also seek to ensure that regulations do not hinder innovation and transformation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: MTI and SPRING, for example, commissioned their review of food manufacturing regulations and the preliminary findings indicated that there is a growing industry interest in novel food ingredients, such as those produced by novel processes or from non-traditional sources.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But there is a need to establish and communicate a regulatory pathway for such novel food ingredients.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is something that is now under regulatory review actively by the Government.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If I can pool some of these ideas together, Aalst Chocolate is a company that exemplifies the enterprise transformation that we seek through these ITMs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I hope Members had a chance to try or sample some of their chocolates in the Members' Room earlier.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: When I last checked, they were all gone, so I am assuming it is because they were consumed.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Established in 2003, as the first Singaporean-owned chocolate manufacturer, Aalst has grown rapidly over the years.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Government agencies have supported Aalst as it enhanced productivity through automation, ventured into new overseas markets and invested in research and innovation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Internationalisation has been at the core of Aalst's business strategy from the very beginning, because Singapore's domestic chocolate consumption clearly cannot sustain its growth.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ninety-eight percent of this company's revenues are from exports, and a key success factor has been branding.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Aalst has used IE Singapore's Global Company Partnership grants to build a brand framework tailored for different markets.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is now an established player, partnering large companies like Dunkin' Donuts, Unilever and Nestle in various markets and projects.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Over the years, the company has also leveraged SPRING's SME Talent Programme to identify the right people for its needs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Dean Ng was one of Aalst's first employees under the SME Talent Programme.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: He joined the company in 2013 as a marketing executive and has since been promoted to a brand manager.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: He works directly with the chief operating officer to develop marketing plans and initiatives to increase sales and brand awareness in all key markets.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Aalst is also in the process of starting student placements under the SkillsFuture Earn and Learn programme.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But the company's growth has also created opportunities for older workers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr David Choy, who is now 62, spent much of his career working in the ship maintenance line.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: At the age of 52, he made the switch to the food manufacturing industry by joining Aalst.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: He upgraded himself through continual training and development, especially as more new equipment were acquired by the company.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Today, he is the "go-to" guy for assistance with Aalst's machinery and he and his life experience is really testimony to the benefits of skills upgrading.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, to sum up, the ITMs encompass a suite of programmes to help our companies scale up and transform.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The aim is to transform every sector, enable enterprises to grow their top-lines and enhance their productivity and competitiveness.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Workers will also benefit from these ITMs because they will gain a clear view of the career pathways in the sector and the skills that are required.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Workers can use the framework to map out their careers, assess skills gaps and tap on programmes, such as the Adapt and Grow Initiative of MOM, to enhance their employability.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Also, TACs like the Singapore Food Manufacturers' Association (SFMA) and SMF will play an important catalytic role as the industry embarks on projects to internationalise, innovate and develop people and technical standards.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann will elaborate on our efforts to enhance the capacity of TACs in this regard.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ms Foo Mee Har asked about the progress and outcomes of the ITMs that have been launched so far and the lessons that have been learnt.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think she is rightly focusing on the implementation elements because that is really where the rub is and that is where we will see the biggest outcomes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It will take time, however, before we can get substantive information to assess the progress and effectiveness of the ITMs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Nonetheless, I would like to emphasise that the ITMs are not static plans.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They will be regularly reviewed, by tracking KPIs, and the plans will be updated and modified as we learn more through implementation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ms Foo also asked if we should prioritise sectors with high-growth potential and established sector partnership structures for the ITMs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But the pace of implementation will, to an extent, depend on the response from the industry and the commitment of the stakeholders.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We also have broad-based schemes to support the needs of companies in the non-ITM sectors as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I just want to say that it is not just about looking at the sectors where we see or assess that there is growth potential, because transformation is needed not just where there is significant growth, but also in sectors where there are other structural challenges, such as, for example, in retail.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Therefore, we need the transformation and the adaptation that we are looking for through the ITMs to make sure the companies in that space are well-positioned for the future.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I want to turn now to the role of the Government and what the Government is doing on its part to respond to some of these changes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As a key enabler, it is important for the Government to be agile in response to changing industry needs, as has been emphasised by Members Mr Yee Chia Hsing and Mr Lee Yi Shyan.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Singapore, as we all know, is well-regarded for its transparency and ease of doing business due to our robust legal system, well-developed infrastructure and skilled talent pool.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have to build on these strengths with a more nimble regulatory posture that safeguards legitimate interests, whilst being more responsive to the changing needs and circumstances of industries.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And if we do this well, it will be another competitive differentiator for Singapore, especially in an era of rapid technological changes and intense competition.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, to that end, we do want a more forward-looking regulatory regime that supports innovation, so that new products and services can be test-bedded and brought to market more quickly.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And this is also in line with the CFE recommendations on regulations, which Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Henry Kwek enquired about.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: At last year's COS, I spoke on the Health Sciences Authority's (HSA's) initiatives to create an enabling regulatory environment for the Medtech industry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Since then, an interagency workgroup led by MTI, comprising HSA, EDB, SPRING, A*STAR and IE Singapore has developed additional recommendations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Applications submitted under this scheme will be prioritised for review, thus shortening turnaround times to register the device.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Patients and healthcare providers will also benefit from earlier access to innovative medical devices.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: With this, companies can consult HSA on the regulatory requirements for devices at the product development stage, well before any formal submissions to register the device for sale or use in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: HSA plans to roll out these initiatives in the second half of this year and will share further details with the industry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: More broadly, to address some of the other points in terms of regulations that have been raised, the Pro-Enterprise Panel (PEP) will continue engaging the industry to identify areas where regulatory processes and compliance costs are of concern to businesses, and work with the agencies to provide solutions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As Miss Cheng Li Hui rightly noted, it is important that we ensure our regulations are not an inadvertent burden to businesses.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I also want to say that our regulations have to keep up with the latest industry trends.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And one example is in the area of land zoning.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In manufacturing, we are seeing more servicisation, and business models are shifting from production-led to service-driven activities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The current guidelines Business 1 zones, which require companies to use at least 60% of their space for core industrial activities, may be too restrictive for some companies, especially those that are already making this transition.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Companies that have offshored their lower value-added activities can also maintain their more knowledge-intensive activities here, while retaining close oversight of their operations overseas.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Market response and feedback to this pilot will be studied, and it will inform any further steps that we take.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Minister for National Development will be elaborating on this approach.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: However, having outlined some of these moves that the Government is making and the general posture that we are taking, I want to caution that even as the Government adopts greater flexibility in regulations, we must remember that we will be entering unchartered waters and we must be prepared that things may not always turn out as planned, in which case, we should be ready to change course or cut losses as such risks are part and parcel of the innovation process.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We should accept them as part of the natural revolution in our system and not always looking for someone to put the blame on when something does not always work out the way we intended it to.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As part of the effort to stay open and connected, we want to help our companies to deepen linkages with overseas networks and partners and seize opportunities in new markets.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is really in the context of our internationalisation efforts.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To ensure seamless support for our enterprises' internationalisation effort, we will strengthen the coordination of our agencies' overseas operations under the consolidated "Singapore Centres".

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These Singapore Centres will serve as the key point of contact for Singapore-based companies when they enter overseas markets, as well as for overseas investors to better understand the business environment in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Singapore Centres will also broaden and deepen our understanding of new markets, including at the city and regional levels, in order to better support our companies as they go overseas, and this is a point that we have emphasised in the course of the CFE studies as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That we need to, well beyond the broad understanding that we have of these markets, and have a much deeper appreciation for second-tier cities, third-tier cities and other regional opportunities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have so far established Singapore Centres in nine key markets and they have been well-received by both local and foreign companies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: A key component of GIA is to build a network of Innovation Launchpads around the world.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Today, our Institutes of Higher Learning, companies and agencies, already have established their own networks overseas.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: GIA will integrate them into one network which companies can then tap on readily to bring their innovations out to relevant markets.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If I may use the example of ViSenze, a local startup providing visual search and image recognition solutions for the e-commerce sector, which has experienced the value of networks first-hand.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In 2016, IE Singapore introduced ViSenze into the Mastercard Start Path accelerator programme in London, a competitive programme geared towards accelerating the growth of promising startups.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Through that programme, ViSenze was exposed to Mastercard's panel of international specialists who linked them up with their network of potential global business leads.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This enabled ViSenze to expand their presence in the US, as well as enlarge their global customer network.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: With GIA, we hope to connect more of our SMEs and startups with the right people and networks in other parts of the world.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These will also enable the best foreign ideas and talent to interface with Singapore companies and to find local partners.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This will not only enrich our innovation ecosystem but also strengthen our value proposition as a base for foreign companies to come here, test-bed new products and then expand into the region.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Charles Chong, Ms Chia Yong Yong and also Mr Leon Perera have asked about our objectives in investing in research and innovation and how we can strengthen the research, innovation and enterprise ecosystem.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As Members have already noted, under the RIE2020 Plan, we have made several shifts to ensure Singapore is well-positioned to harness technology and innovation to drive our next phase of economic growth.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Then there are some fundings set aside for the white-space elements.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Second, to tighten linkages between our R&D capabilities and industry needs, we have increased funding for public-private research collaborations under the Industry Alignment Fund (IAF).

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, that is going to bring the public sector and the private sector closer together.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Thirdly, to spur the best ideas, we have increased the proportion of competitive funding that is open to all public research performers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These shifts combine to bring about a significant directional move in our RIE ecosystem.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Perera asked how we can leverage competitions as a means to develop IP.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: SPRING has worked with partners, such as the National University of Singapore (NUS), the National Research Foundation (NRF) and the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), and incubators to co-organise startup competitions judged by angel investors and venture capitalists at events, such as Tech Venture 2016 and InnoFest 2016.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The winning teams win prize money and a validation of their business plans and execution ability.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong has asked about the structural changes that we will effect to achieve our objectives in research and innovation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Charles Chong has also asked about A*STAR's reorganisation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As Members would recall, as Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean, in his capacity as Chairman of NRF, announced in February this year, A*STAR has embarked on a transformation effort to bring R&D innovations to industry more quickly and in a more targeted and collaborative manner.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: A*STAR's research has always been geared towards meeting the needs of industry and society.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They have always had that as their mission orientation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: However, with the gathering pace and complexity of technological advances, more and more innovations are occurring at the interstices of disciplines.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, companies must increasingly draw on multidisciplinary capabilities to develop new solutions and they need to do that with greater speed.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: A*STAR will move towards more flexible, multidisciplinary programmes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These programmes will also be term-limited, meaning that A*STAR will then have the flexibility to start new programmes in line with evolving industry interests and needs, as well as phase out programmes which are no longer effective in meeting the needs of industry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And this is an inherent flexibility that we want to build up in the institution so that they can be more responsive to the market.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Equally importantly, these programmes will provide companies with a convenient modality to collaborate with multiple public research performers on complex, multidisciplinary challenges.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: One example of such innovation is in the manufacturing sector and it is nano imprinting.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I just want to say a little bit about it because it is a bit technical.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I, myself, am just grappling with understanding some of the fundamentals of it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But it basically taps on capabilities, such as nano-fabrication, simulation and modelling.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This process enables the creation of textures and patterns at the nano-meter-scale, that is, 10 to the power of minus nine, so as to impart special properties to materials.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Examples of such properties include anti-reflection, adhesive and water repellents.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It can be applied to materials, such as plastics, glass and metals.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Given the growing industry interest in this area, A*STAR has set up the Nano-imprint Foundry that is hosted at the Institute of Materials Research and Engineering (IMRE), which pools together capabilities from IMRE, as well as the Institute of High Performance Computing (IHPC) and the Data Science Institute (DSI).

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They are pooling different resources from various institutes together in order to take this nano-imprinting effort forward.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong and Mr Perera also asked about the economic impact of our public R&D activities and how this is monitored.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We track a spectrum of performance indicators to ensure that our investments generate good outcomes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Thirdly, we track A*STAR's Growing Enterprises Through Technology Upgrade (GET-Up) programme, which is really a programme which provides SMEs with support in technology adoption through the secondment of researchers and technology road-mapping.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Collectively, these outcomes suggest and indicate that we have been able to get good value out of our investments in R&D.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But it is not something that we take for granted because there is always more that can be done and that is why I will elaborate on the range of measures that we are undertaking.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Importantly, these measures have also anchored investments and good jobs in Singapore, as well as uplifted the capabilities of local companies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Some of these are hard to quantify but if you ask the EDB officers, if you ask others in the industry, the qualitative engagement and traction within the industry have been very strong.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong also asked about how we can assure that IP generated from public sector R&D is managed well to reap economic and societal benefits.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Fundamentally, we want our IP policy to ensure that we create and capture value for Singapore through the IPs that we generate.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Recognising that companies have different commercialisation needs, public agencies adopt different approaches to engage industry that include licensing, that is, exclusive or non-exclusive licensing, and also the assignment of IP.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Conditions may be imposed to ensure that companies are, in fact, committed to creating value from the IP.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are making publicly-funded IP more accessible to companies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: With this, companies will have greater clarity over IP ownership practices and standardised and simplified IP negotiations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: More importantly, companies will be able to bring innovative products and services quickly to market and reap value.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will share more information on the National IP Protocol in the second quarter of the year.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Henry Kwek have asked how we plan to implement the CFE recommendations on lead demand.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We want to leverage more lead demand to catalyse innovation and business opportunities for companies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Government is investing in several areas which are both significant from a domestic needs viewpoint and also in terms of growth possibilities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These include healthcare, urban solutions, security and the Internet-of-Things.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These are also areas of opportunity for our smaller and innovative enterprises so that they can build their capabilities and strengthen their track record.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is especially so as the Government can be a valuable reference customer for SMEs which are seeking to capture more deals and venture overseas.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To help our SMEs participate in these opportunities, we will adopt a more targeted, systematic approach to using lead demand, through an enhanced Partnerships for Capability Transformation (PACT) programme which we have already been doing.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And this new programme will be called PACT through Government Lead Demand, or Gov-PACT.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Today, EDB and SPRING's PACT programme have the collaboration among large organisations and local SMEs, something that some Members mentioned.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We want to build on that to foster more collaboration between Government agencies and SMEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Under the Gov-PACT programme, SPRING will work with agencies to put out calls for proposals where SMEs can co-innovate in identified strategic areas, with the Government committing to procure the solution if the specifications are met.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Through this programme, SMEs will be given opportunities to develop, test-bed and validate new solutions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann will elaborate further.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: One sector that has benefited from the Government Lead Demand approach is the clean energy sector.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The SolarNova programme aggregates public sector demand for solar photovoltaic (PV) panels, and it has catalysed our solar PV industry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing had asked about the future plans for the clean energy sector in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The clean energy industry here has grown a small base of about 10 companies in 2007 to around 100 companies last year.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And we are committed to developing it further, through a number of initiatives.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will enhance Singapore's position as a living lab and extend the use of lead demand to help more Singapore-based companies build their track record and pursue regional opportunities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will maximise deployable space in our dense urban setting, by increasing the use of building integrated PV.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will also explore the application of regulatory sandboxes to microgrids and floating PVs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The sector will also help address Singapore's energy security, competitiveness and sustainability needs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have already seen the growth of home-grown enterprises like the Singapore solar company Cleantech Solar, which has developed capabilities in roof-top solar system integration and remote monitoring from Singapore, and it has ventured into the region.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This includes a roof-top solar project that Coca Cola recently established at its bottling facility in Cambodia.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is Coca Cola's first flagship solar project in Southeast Asia and its system performance is being monitored and optimised in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And if Members look at it, the water feature is in the shape of a Coca Cola bottle.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is noteworthy that this growth has been achieved without any subsidies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Rather, it has been aided by the cost of solar power coming down and modular efficiencies improving with technological developments.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As a result, solar power has become competitive against the price of electricity from the grid which we also do not subsidise.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The global impetus to reduce carbon emissions is another contributory factor.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Energy Market Authority (EMA) has studied this matter quite carefully as renewable energy resources like solar are intermittent in nature and, therefore, they can affect our system stability.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: However, specifically and in response to Assoc Prof Daniel Goh's point, unlike some jurisdictions, we have not set binding targets for renewable energy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The reason is because often, such binding targets result in subsidies and other measures in the effort to get that target and, in the process, they distort price signals and market behaviours.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Instead, our policy has been to ensure that energy, regardless of the source of generation, is priced right to fully reflect the cost of generation and then we let the market work out the equilibrium.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is why we have avoided Feed-in Tariffs that are common in other jurisdictions, with binding renewable energy targets.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Feed-in Tariffs subsidise solar electricity by pricing it higher than electricity from the grid.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Instead, what we have done is invested in the development of solar PV technology and the result showed that this has served us well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, even the industry players, many of whom are local enterprises, have given me similar feedback.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On Mr Yee Chia Hsing's point, I should clarify that grid charges are not levied on solar PV owners or any other generation source for that manner.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The electricity price that we pay, there is a grid charge component.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That does not go to the company or the entity generating the electricity.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That goes to the grid company and, in our case, SP PowerGrid.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is to cover the cost of building and maintaining the national power grid.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, whether you are a conventional generator of electricity or a solar generator, you are basically getting the price that is net off the grid charge.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing also suggested tiering electricity tariffs to penalise the heaviest electricity consumers with higher rates and then use that to subsidise lower-income households.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As a practical matter, I want to say that such an approach is quite problematic.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For example, how would you determine the tiers for such differential pricing because the circumstances for households and their needs vary quite widely even if they live in the same type of housing.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our approach is to price electricity right fully from the first electron and then we provide targeted assistance through the tiered U-Save rebates.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The outcome, in some ways, from an equity point of view, is not unlike the intent that Mr Yee has in his suggestion.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Henry Kwek noted that as Asia urbanises, the demand for urban solutions will rise.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This goes beyond energy infrastructure to water, waste management, telecommunications and transportation infrastructure.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is about the right scale for SMEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, Memiontec, for example, is a company that has built deep capabilities in water asset developments in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They have capabilities in engineering, procurement, construction management and operations and maintenance works for water reclamation and water treatment.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In Singapore, they built a wastewater treatment plant to clean water before it is discharged from our Semakau landfill.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Last year, the company also ventured successfully into infrastructure development overseas because they secured a deal to build, own and operate a water treatment plant that would convert water from Jakarta's West Flood Canal into clean water for Jakarta's residents.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Memiontec is keen to scale up and secure more of such projects.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We want more of our companies, especially our SMEs, to be able to tap on these growing opportunities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But their expansion is constrained by limited access to project financing for small projects.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Typically, commercial lenders are less prepared to provide financing to SMEs unless they put up personal guarantees or recourse to the company's assets.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: At the other end of the spectrum, infrastructure developers who are working on large overseas projects face a different kind of challenge.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Commercial lenders typically require insurance cover against sovereign risks of emerging markets, while foreign developers rely on their respective export credit agencies for such insurance coverage.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The focus is on the development of deep skills for our people and building enterprise capabilities for higher productivity, innovation and internationalisation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These are priorities that we have been working on for many years, and we will continue to do so in the context of a more dynamic environment that we are in today.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And we believe that, collectively, these efforts will help ensure that our economy remains vibrant with thriving businesses and good opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing, please take your cut on helping SMEs to compete effectively.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Chairman, SMEs are an important part of our economy.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Some of the common reasons cited are mainly implementation costs of the new technology, lack of training and know-how or, simply, reluctance to change.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: On that note, I would like to ask what the Ministry is doing to help our SMEs increase their competitiveness and capture new opportunities both in the local and global markets.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   This year's Budget has placed key focus on innovation and internationalisation in the future economy.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The saying goes: A thousand-mile journey begins with the first step.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: With clear direction, the next step is to achieve this in the fastest way possible.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: With regard to innovation capability, let us first look at what SMEs have done.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SCCCI) conducted a survey on innovation efforts of enterprises.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: A total of 233 enterprises took part, with SMEs making up 98.8% of respondents.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, only 15% collaborated with public research institutes.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Very few are able to recruit researchers to handle R&D.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: If they wish to improve their innovation capability, they need to strengthen the collaboration with research institutes.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Moving on, we urge more local enterprises to leverage the Government's research resources.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Technology innovation is not a matter of difficulty, but the crux is whether there are practical applications.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, assistance would be forthcoming to 100 companies every year.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This is an astronomical figure, compared to the 100 companies that would get relevant assistance within a year.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We hope that A*STAR could work with the trade associations to develop technology applications that could be shared with certain industries.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Making the benefits accessible to a wider group would assuredly be a more effective way of encouraging technology adoption.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that this International Partnership Fund would cast its sights for returns over a longer 10-year period or beyond that.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Local enterprises which venture abroad to form joint ventures in other countries or tender for projects, need to gear up on sufficient project experience.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In November last year, I led a business mission to Myanmar and we were warmly received by the Myanmar Chinese Chamber of Commerce.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The Myanmar government also invited us to invest in their infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The Government must allow local SMEs to participate in these projects and have the opportunity to become main contractors.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore SMEs which work with Government-linked companies and MNCs could gain in experience, improve on standards and chalk up a creditable track record.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This could raise their competitiveness in the global marketplace.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This, in fact, is the most effective way to help local enterprises internationalise.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Last month, Minister S Iswaran and his team came for a dialogue at the SCCCI; it was attended by trade association leaders and business representatives from more than 20 industries.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We discovered that businesses still have certain misunderstandings on how to tackle specific operational details.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Moving ahead, we should organise more sessions for trade associations and industry associations to establish better communication with Government officials, bringing these misunderstandings to a minimum.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Improving the competitiveness of local enterprises is our common objective.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In order for this objective to be achieved, the Government charts policies and offers resources; trade associations participate and provide useful suggestions; enterprises and entrepreneurs, however, assume the most important role.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Innovation and internationalisation basically call for a departure from one's comfort zone, the boldness to try out new things and, in the process, seek perfection.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This is where enterprises cannot totally rely on external sources of strength but on individual hard work.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, the Budget has a slew of extensive targeted measures to support industries and companies in their medium- to long-term effort to improve their businesses' productivity and performances.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In light of this, has the Ministry tracked and monitored the performances of SMEs which received assistance last year?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will MTI provide a progress report showing which sectors have benefited and shown improvement and which, despite all measures and assistance, have yet to yield any results?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What measures can be taken to improve this sector's productivity?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In regard to the Government's Enabling Growth and Innovation measures, besides providing financial support, can the Government take on a greater role in supporting SMEs in their overseas ventures by helping them leverage its network?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister earlier alluded to their effort in doing so, but probably we can be more pervasive in this effort.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With today's economy, many SMEs may need more handholding to sustain themselves.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Despite all the financial assistance rendered by the Government, some SMEs may end up winding down their businesses and the workers will be adversely affected.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Government consider working with the Labour Movement to explore ways to assist these affected workers leverage programmes, such as the "Adapt and Grow" programme, and transit into new employment before the company winds down?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: These workers can plan and start to upskill and reskill to enhance their employability earlier.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: All the Government's support and assistance should be directed to sunrise companies or future-ready companies with potential for growth.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Government evaluate the situation and circumstances in which SMEs are given assistance to ensure accountability?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: However, there are concerns that our micro and heartland enterprise, such as those in our Housing and Development Board (HDB) estates, are being left behind.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This is akin to "putting old wine in a new bottle".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The bottle looks attractive but, over time, it will lose its appeal, because the inside has not changed at all.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Many of the heartland businesses are run by the older generation bosses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Their shops have been there since the flats were built, and they abide by the traditional, conventional way of running business.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This can eventually lead to their business getting phased out as the age group of their customers get younger and the customers are flocking online and elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What is the Government doing to help them?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Heartland businesses contribute to a rustic charm within the neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is something unique to Singapore's public housing that we will rarely find elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Moreover, the convenient locations of these shops increase connectivity within the neighbourhood and are popular with the elderly and less-mobile.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I hope the Government can do more to help these heartland shops stay abreast of the times and remain relevant to the residents in the neighbourhood.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Some of the measures introduced to support our SMEs to level up with the industry may not benefit these businesses.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Can I know what plans the Ministry has to support these micro enterprises?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: One, periodic proactive communications of schemes and roadshow at the localised level.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Move the satellite SME Centres to the localised level like the specific malls or even the town centres.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This would give better access for the business owners to participate and seek assistance.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Two, provide a suite of modules where different businesses can plug and play to adapt in order to enhance their efficiency.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Three, customise some relevant SkillsFuture courses to accommodate the long working hours and the working conditions of the staff in the micro enterprises so that they can work and also successfully upskill.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Lastly, I would like to ask the Minister on the scheme of the SME Working Capital Loan introduced last year.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Have the banks been forthcoming since the scheme was introduced?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Were there good success rates for application from non-traditional business models?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In its press release on the matter, the Competition Commission acknowledged that there could be cost savings for Town Councils should they engage third-party lift maintenance contractors for various brands as compared to procuring lift maintenance services from original lift installers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, The Straits Times noted that the original complaint was made to the Competition Commission about EM Services, a joint venture between HDB and CapitaLand, sparking an investigation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The long duration of time between the initial complaint and the resolution of the matter would have had potentially significant cost implications for Town Councils, which could have secured favourable maintenance rates from third-party maintenance providers, had a resolution to this matter being achieved earlier.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Section 67 of the Competition Act provides for interim measures in the midst of investigations when the Commission believes a section 47 prohibition has been infringed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The essential ingredients of instituting such interim measures are if the matter is an urgent one to prevent serious injury to a person or a category of persons or, secondly, simply to protect the public interest.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would appear that section 67 could have been employed against any lift company intentionally withholding the supply of lift parts under either of these two limbs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The high incidence of high-rise living in Singapore and, separately, a spate of lift incidents from 2015 in particular, brought home the point about the public interest in a very real way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Not only would safety concerns and the public interest have been addressed, Town Councils could potentially have saved hundreds of thousands of dollars, thanks to more competitive lift contracts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Who was consulted and why did the Competition Commission choose this method of resolution and not impose interim measures?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Biosimilars are engineered to have the same therapeutic effect as an existing drug − they call it a "reference product" − with no clinically meaningful differences in safety and effectiveness.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: They work within existing intellectual property frameworks, so have the potential market impact of what would have been called a generic drug, especially if clinical trials show equivalence.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: These are a potential disruptive innovation to traditional pharma markets as well as pharma producers in the first-world as well as in Asia.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: How do we position Singapore's own biologics and drug development sector amidst this changing landscape?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: What are the challenges and opportunities for our Singapore workers and Singapore industries?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Charles Chong, you have two cuts, can you take them together?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Singapore's manufacturing sector has always been a strong anchor for our economy while also being at the same time a key source of our competitiveness which provides us with links to the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Our manufacturing sector has been a good source of growth and a provider of valuable jobs for many years.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: It will, however, be challenging for our manufacturing companies to stay relevant and competitive in the current global manufacturing landscape.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Technological advances in the industry have made things far more efficient today and the employment of technology in the form of robotics and additive manufacturing has become more widespread.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: The use of industrial robots in manufacturing can also help to increase the overall operational efficiency in a wide range of areas.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Robots can operate with much more precision and consistency than human operators and also can be employed in processes or instances where it may not be optimal to deploy a human.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: On the other hand, additive manufacturing injects greater speed and flexibility in the product development and prototyping process.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: It can also help to shorten supply chains so that the final product is ready more quickly.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: The Government has always encouraged our companies to embrace change and transform themselves.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: In this particular context, it will mean being open to tapping on these advanced manufacturing technologies for new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: However, we all know that change is difficult.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Some companies may see the need to transform but do not know how to go about doing so.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Others may be unsure about whether it will be worth the money to invest in these new technologies and change the way they do business.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: They may also be worried about business downtime.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Next, I would like to touch on startups and our innovation ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Startups are becoming increasingly prominent in the global economy, both as creators of economic value and as disruptors of existing industries.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Many countries are placing increasing emphasis on attracting and retaining global entrepreneurial talent to catalyse a vibrant startup culture, much like Silicon Valley, which is a melting pot of the best and brightest tech minds from all over the world.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: In Singapore, we are in the process of building an increasingly vibrant startup ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: The CFE report speaks of world-renowned universities and research institutions, and we even teach entrepreneurial skills in our schools now.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Many young people want to start up their own businesses, and this is a very encouraging sign for our economy.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: CFE noted that a vibrant startup ecosystem requires capable entrepreneurs with a global outlook.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: However, these should be individuals who are prepared to anchor their businesses in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: This scheme allows eligible foreigners to start and operate a new business in Singapore.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan's speech on Consumer Protection submitted to MTI.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Emerging markets are forecasted to have a larger growth of 5%-7%.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Most emerging markets have requirements to build infrastructures to cater for energy, connectivity and basic needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: They have needs in areas where we consider jobs within traditional markets in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: With limited land space, there will come a time when we have maximised our built infrastructure and the need for each subsequent mega project will be at least a decade or two apart.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: An example of good leading efforts in this respect is the Japanese business community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Japanese companies have capitalised on their technology and expertise to undertake infrastructure-related projects in ASEAN and the African continent, where the capabilities of these emerging markets are at their infancy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: It not only created jobs for their people but also further strengthened their capabilities and learnings through diversity against the various country backdrops.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: These are some common reasons that senior PMEs received when asked to vacate their work positions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: It is possible for some individuals that these reasons cited may bear truth, but what if the senior PMEs can still contribute in significant ways?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Would they have a role in the workforce and social scene?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I have met successful examples of senior PMEs who switched industries, had practical expectations of remunerations and some ventured to become new entrepreneurs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The first, in last year's COS, I have raised and would ask the Ministry again to consider having senior PMEs with experience and international exposure to mentor the SMEs and startups.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Functional experiences under the diverse business conditions are useful knowledge to be shared and imparted.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: PMEs can learn new business areas or skills from the startups with fresh, new concepts and, likewise, SMEs can be taken to higher grounds with the network and executional insights.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: So, I would say a platform to match the requirements and supply of this talent pool is thus essential.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The second area − supplement workforce in specific sectors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Healthcare and education are key growth areas and would continue to face staff shortages.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: As a society, we constantly demand more care and concern for our young and old.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Being a senior, one is probably best placed to understand the mindset and needs of others in that same age group.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: In contrast to our younger workforce, our seniors will have some time, flexibility and impetus to undergo training and transformation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: They can also supplement the social service sector with their people management skills and knowledge.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Senior PMEs may be less constrained by familial burden as compared to young couples at the early stages of their career and family lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Those who have had prior overseas assignments or managed regional roles would be well acquainted with such postings.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: They can bring forth the local establishments from Singapore with desires to anchor overseas and broaden their markets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Existing jobs will be impacted and new job opportunities will emerge.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How will the Government help to prepare the employees?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Continuous education is one of the keys and, certainly, SkillsFuture will be helpful.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But there is only so much time and money one has to spend on furthering their education.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It will be helpful if employees in the affected industries can have a heads-up on what particular areas they should focus on and which skills and courses they can contribute to their new roles.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Will there be, for example, 23 manpower ITMs, too?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: To help young Singaporeans plug into business networks regionally, it takes language skills, region-specific knowledge, things which are not in the textbooks.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: What steps are we taking to help bring our people up to speed?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Are we planning courses in regional languages, regional cultural nuances, even courses on how to interact persuasively in a regional business setting so as to shorten the learning curve and maximise opportunities?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: They ask pointed questions about how I am running the company which I am not comfortable with.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: A very telling example about the various issues we face with internationalisation and what would be needed to overcome them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: What could be considered an aggressive mode of discussion could be the cultural norm somewhere else.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Further, to have a successful product, we would need to understand the pain points different markets have.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They are the base from which many brands have emerged and we hope and believe many more great Singapore companies will grow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The concerns of SMEs are also the Government's concerns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Supporting SMEs is very much at the front and centre of the CFE report as well as this year's Budget.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It will also be a key focus of the MTI family in the months and years to come.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The feedback from SMEs falls into three main categories.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: First, the need for assistance to cope with challenges, both immediate and in the longer term; second, where to go and who to approach for assistance and, third, how to transform themselves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We are making it easier for SMEs to receive assistance and we are doing more to help SMEs implement step-by-step plans if they wish to transform.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For the first category, in terms of how to cope with challenges, several Ministers have already spoken about them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Hence, I shall address the question of whether we can make it easier for SMEs to benefit from our support schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: First, by changing the way Government agencies work with one another to support SMEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our economic agencies are largely organised based on function and, with a few exceptions, not by industry type.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But SMEs have told us that if they knew that there was one specific agency in charge of their industry, they would feel more assured.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They will know the needs of the entire industry are considered holistically.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is why we have organised our industry strategies into ITMs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We now have one lead agency for each industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: SMEs can think of each ITM as a guide to the key shifts in the industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It lays out the practical steps they can take to transform their businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There are four major themes: to improve productivity, innovate, internationalise as well as to develop the skills of our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: To address Ms K Thanaletchimi's question, we do have indicators to track the progress of the ITMs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At the national level, we track indicators, such as value-add and value-add per worker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At the sector level, each ITM is tailored to the specific needs of the sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have sector-specific indicators to track progress in productivity, innovation, internationalisation and in developing the skills of our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Food Services ITM helps SMEs address a key challenge − their heavy reliance on manpower.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is made more acute by an ageing workforce and the fact that many prefer to work in other sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As part of the ITM, food services SMEs will be supported in their adoption of technology, as well as the development of productive and innovative business formats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: An example is Omakase Burger, a gourmet burger restaurant chain that specialises in smashed burgers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As some foodies might know, an artisan burger is especially juicy and delicious because the meat patties are shaped by hand and not compressed by machine.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: So, a key challenge for Omakase was that a lot of the food processing was manual.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Whether the business can grow depends crucially on how many skilled chefs it can hire and, as many of us know, this is one of the biggest bottlenecks in the F&B industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Is there no machine that can replicate the taste and texture of a hand-shaped burger patty?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It turns out there is, one that uses vacuum suction technology instead of straightforward compression.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: With the support of SPRING's Capability Development Grant (CDG), the company was able to automate its processing kitchen in 2016.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Now, Omakase can make more of the same delicious burgers and think of expanding operations and growing its top line, without having to find more chefs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Ms K Thanaletchimi asked how we can improve productivity in our retail sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is addressed in the Retail ITM which sets out to drive greater productivity through technology and shared platforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: An example, SPRING has worked with retailers to get them to use self-check-out counters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The former cashiers were redeployed to new stores or reassigned to other duties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: E-commerce and omni-channel sales will also help retailers to better meet customers' needs and allow them to do more with a lean workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Retail ITM encourages and supports SMEs and their workers to take advantage of these strategies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: SPRING is working with Workforce SG to conduct master classes on omni-channel retailing and digital marketing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As Ms Foo Mee Har pointed out, there are potential synergies among the different industries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: That is why we are adopting a cluster approach for our ITM efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For instance, we will identify and develop common digital solutions and automation technologies that can be applied across industries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: And we will work with SMEs to deploy them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As an example, within the Lifestyle cluster, there is Techmetics, a robotics and IT solutions company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It provides common automation solutions to the Food Services and Hotels industries and has worked with SPRING and the Singapore Tourism Board to deploy these solutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In restaurants like Kinsa Sushi, guests can place their orders through Techmetics' iPad ordering solution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Their food is then delivered by Techi, a robotic waiter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The company also adapted Techi to meet the needs of hotels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For instance, Techi is at work in Park Avenue @ Rochester, delivering room service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The robot is able to take the lift, travel to the guest's doorstep and notify him through a phone call that the food has arrived.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Techi helps the food services and hotels industries do more without needing more staff.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It also saves ageing workers from having to perform physically tedious or repetitive tasks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It also means that homegrown tech companies can showcase their solutions and, hopefully, achieve greater success.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We look forward to supporting more SMEs adopt such win-win solutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We often hear that SMEs are not sure whom to approach for help.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Miss Cheryl Chan have raised similar concerns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We did not just reorganise the delivery of assistance in the form of ITMs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As a first touchpoint, we have our SME Centres for SMEs, including our heartland and micro enterprises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As a first stop, the SME Centres provide customised business advice and help SMEs better understand Government initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Last year, we also enhanced our SME Centres to provide business diagnosis and run capability workshops for SMEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Complementing the SME Centres is our SME Portal, which serves as the first online touchpoint for SMEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The portal offers Government and commercial information useful for SMEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It also lists services suitable for SMEs at various business stages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is a showcase of easily adoptable technology solutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It will include A*STAR's ready-to-go (RTG) technologies as well as IMDA's prequalified Infocomm and Media (ICM) solutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These can help companies improve inventory and asset tracking processes, supply chain management and planning processes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For SMEs looking to embark on a transformation journey, we are more than willing to meet them halfway by providing step-by-step, customised assistance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing asked how our SMEs can increase their competitiveness, given the rapid technological changes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have taken steps to help SMEs enhance their technological capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These include improving their access to technology solutions and helping them identify and implement the ones best suited to their needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: First, for SMEs that require specific help to identify how technology can support their business strategies, A*STAR can help them develop an operation and technology roadmap (OTR).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This involves a customised, step-by-step guide of what companies need to do to better leverage technology in their operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Second, SMEs that wish to develop, prototype and test new products can tap on our new Tech Access initiative.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They will get access to A*STAR's installed base of specialised equipment on advanced manufacturing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This will help them build capabilities in the use of advanced machine tools, new processes, prototyping and testing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: SMEs will also receive user training and advice from A*STAR to optimise the effectiveness of the equipment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As Mr Thomas Chua has noted, TACs are important partners to help us leverage R&D to uplift the capabilities of our SMEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: A*STAR has worked with TACs, such as the Singapore Precision Engineering and Technology Association (SPETA) and the Singapore School Transport Association (SSTA), on specific R&D projects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: A*STAR will continue to engage TACs on specific R&D projects, as well as to help them tap on new initiatives like the Tech Access and Tech Depot.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We also want to strengthen our support for SME capability development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: SPRING's CDG is one of our key support schemes for this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It supports SMEs to take on upgrading projects across 10 key business areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: To make it easier for companies to do capability development, SPRING simplified the application process for grants below $30,000 in 2015.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This has received a positive response and, as a result, many more companies today have been able to benefit from the grant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We are constantly looking for ways to broaden and deepen our support for capability development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This year, we will strengthen our support in product development by extending the grant coverage to small batch production.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Currently, most of our support efforts focus on helping companies develop their products at the R&D and prototyping phase.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But for products to be commercially scalable, companies need to ensure that the product design and manufacturing process are optimised.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We hope the expansion in grant coverage will help to co-share risks associated with this early stage of production and help our SMEs to scale.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Beyond this, we will be taking steps to better drive innovation among our SMEs and startups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Today, there are efforts by various Government agencies to work with companies to co-develop innovative solutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Participating companies can also tap on SPRING's CDG to fund part of the cost involved in the development of new technologies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But we recognise that SMEs and startups still face uncertainty of securing the procurement contract after investing time and resources at the development stages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We help more SMEs and startups participate in Government projects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For example, the procurement process for projects under this scheme will be broken into stages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: An SME or startup will be eligible to move on to the next stage once the current stage proves successful.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This will reduce the risk and investment for the SME.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Through the field trials, vTrium was able to prove that their flexible panels work well on curved surfaces and vertical building facades and in a tropical climate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We hope that this initiative will give SMEs and startups the opportunity to engage the Government as a valuable reference customer and build their track record.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Mr Thomas Chua also asked about how SMEs can participate in the $700 million worth of construction projects that MOF is bringing forward.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Ministry of National Development will be speaking about this at their COS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We also want to ensure that we have healthy, competitive and efficient markets in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is the goal of the Competition Commission of Singapore (CCS) and I thank Mr Pritam Singh for his question.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: CCS administers the Competition Act, which allows it to issue an interim measures directive to businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is provided there are reasonable grounds to suspect an infringement of the Competition Act and if there is urgency to act for the purpose of either protecting the public interest or preventing serious, irreparable damage to a business.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We would like to clarify that in the case of EM Services brought up by Mr Pritam Singh, CCS' view was that the threshold for an interim measures directive, in other words, that third-party contractors had suffered serious and irreparable damage as required under the Competition Act, had not been reached.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I would also like to highlight that safety concerns of the public would have been considered by BCA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: With regard to public consultation, it is standard practice for CCS to seek feedback from industry stakeholders on a company's proposed commitments as they are in the best position to assess if the commitments will address the competition issue.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: CCS would consider the feedback in deciding whether to accept the commitments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I have explained how the MTI family assists SMEs, how we are making it easier for SMEs to obtain assistance, and how we are moving to help more SMEs in a customised, step-by-step manner to transform.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But, given the sheer number of active SMEs in our economy, the Government alone cannot help all businesses transform.
